title: The Verb To Be: Am, Is, Are
summary: The verb 'to be' is the most important verb in English. Learn when to use am, is and are, and how to make negatives and questions.

sections.p: Use 'am' only with I. Use 'is' with he, she, it and one person or thing. Use 'are' with you, we, they and more than one person or thing. We use 'to be' to talk about names, age, jobs, feelings, places and descriptions.
In speaking and informal writing, we usually join the pronoun and the verb: I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're. The meaning is exactly the same, but it sounds more natural.

ex.mean: Saying your age (in English we use 'be' for age).
Saying what we are to each other.

sections.p: To make a negative, add 'not' after am, is or are. The short forms are 'I'm not', 'isn't' and 'aren't'. There is no short form 'amn't'.

ex.mean: Saying you do not feel tired.
Saying a man does not have this job.
Telling someone they arrived on time.

sections.p: To ask a question, put am, is or are before the subject. Give short answers with the verb: 'Yes, I am.' 'No, she isn't.' In positive short answers, do not use the short form: say 'Yes, I am', not 'Yes, I'm'.

ex.mean: Asking if something costs a lot.

tip: Remember the pattern I-am, he-she-it-is, you-we-they-are. Say it like a little song three times and it will stay in your head.

quiz.en: A: Are you a teacher? B: Yes, ___
